html:
The Long March was the retreat of the Chinese Red Army from southeast China to the northwest, from October 1934 to October 1935. The Communists escaped the armies of Chiang Kai-shek and settled around Yan'an (Yenan) in Shaanxi, but only about one in ten of those who set out arrived.

The Communists had run a small state in the hills of Jiangxi. In 1934 Chiang's Nationalists closed in on it with rings of forts. In October about 86,000 soldiers and party workers broke out to the west. At the Xiang River they lost perhaps half their number. In January 1935, at a meeting in Zunyi, Mao Zedong began his rise to the leadership. The army then crossed the mountains, rivers and swamps of western China, fighting Nationalists and warlords. It covered about 9,000 km in a year, though the distance is disputed. Fewer than 10,000 reached northern Shaanxi.

As a campaign it was a defeat, but it saved the Communist Party and became its founding story. From Yan'an the party grew during the war with Japan, and in 1949 it won the civil war. Veterans of the march, among them Deng Xiaoping, ruled China for half a century.
